title: SRE and Infrastructure Architecture in Plain English
summary: Connect business-critical services, reliability targets, dependencies and operational evidence before choosing technology controls.
plain_language_explanation: Architecture defines how a service should meet business outcomes under normal load, failure and change. SRE turns those expectations into measurable reliability objectives, operational evidence and controlled improvement.
quick_check: Why is component uptime alone insufficient to prove a service is reliable?

title: Service Reliability Architecture, SLIs, SLOs and Error Budgets
summary: Translate business expectations into measurable service-level indicators, objectives and reliability decision boundaries.
objective: Design reliability around user-visible service outcomes, quantified tolerance for failure and explicit architecture dependencies.
body_outline: Identify critical user journeys and business impact before selecting reliability metrics.
Choose SLIs that represent user-visible success such as availability, latency, correctness or freshness.
Set SLOs that balance reliability with delivery velocity and economic constraints.
Use error budgets as decision input rather than as permission to ignore incidents.
Map dependency failure modes, capacity limits and recovery assumptions to each service objective.
Keep SLO ownership, measurement windows and exception decisions auditable.

title: Observability Architecture and Actionable Monitoring
summary: Design telemetry that distinguishes symptoms from causes and helps operators detect, triage and explain service degradation.
objective: Build monitoring around service symptoms, capacity and dependency evidence while minimizing unactionable alert noise.
body_outline: Prioritize user-facing symptoms such as latency and errors over raw infrastructure counters alone.
Track traffic, errors, latency and saturation alongside dependency health.
Use logs, metrics and traces as complementary evidence rather than interchangeable telemetry.
Define alert ownership, severity and response expectation before enabling an alert.
Avoid static thresholds that ignore normal workload patterns and service objectives.
Correlate observability data with deployments, configuration changes and incidents.

title: Resilience Engineering, Incident Learning and Architecture Trade-offs
summary: Design operations around failure containment, controlled response, post-incident learning and explicit architecture trade-offs.
architecture_notes: Resilience requires more than redundancy. It requires defined failure domains, capacity headroom, dependency isolation, tested recovery paths, observability, incident roles and feedback into architecture. Postmortems should explain contributing conditions and durable corrective actions without reducing complex failure to individual blame.
failure_modes: redundant components share the same dependency and fail together
capacity headroom disappears during maintenance or regional degradation
alerts detect infrastructure noise but miss user-visible failure
runbooks assume dependencies that are unavailable during the incident
postmortem actions address symptoms but not systemic causes
architecture decisions are made without documenting reliability, cost and operational trade-offs
enterprise_design_notes: Use architecture decision records, service dependency maps, SLO/error-budget evidence, capacity models, recovery tests, incident reviews and tracked corrective actions as one operating system for reliability.

title: Read-Only Service Reliability Evidence Pack
summary: Build a timestamped architecture/SRE evidence pack without changing production topology, monitoring or reliability policy.
objective: Collect enough evidence to review service reliability before proposing architecture or SRE changes.
steps: Confirm service owner, business criticality and approved review scope.
Record current SLI/SLO definitions and measurement windows if they exist.
Inventory critical dependencies and known single points of failure.
Review recent latency, error, traffic and saturation evidence without changing alerts.
Review recent incidents, recurring failure patterns and open corrective actions.
Document reliability gaps, evidence confidence and required owner/change approvals before recommending action.
expected_result: A read-only dossier linking service objectives, dependencies, telemetry, incidents and architecture risks without changing production.
rollback: Not required; prescribed activities are read-only.

title: Cross-Layer Reliability Incident Decision Tree
summary: Separate user impact, dependency failure, capacity saturation, change regression and observability gaps before remediation.
diagnostic_order: Confirm actual user impact and affected service objective before focusing on infrastructure symptoms.
Build a timeline of alerts, deployments, configuration changes and dependency events.
Check latency, errors, traffic and saturation across service and dependency boundaries.
Distinguish capacity exhaustion, shared-dependency failure and recent-change regression.
Identify observability blind spots when evidence cannot explain the symptom.
Escalate topology, failover, scaling or policy changes through approved incident/change authority.
escalation_boundary: Do not change SLOs, alert thresholds, scaling, failover policy, routing, capacity reservations or production topology solely to make an incident metric appear healthy.

title: Infrastructure Architecture and SRE Assessment
summary: Scenario assessment covering SLOs, observability, resilience and incident learning.

assessment_items.question: Why should an SLO describe user-visible service behavior rather than only server uptime?
assessment_items.answer: A service can have healthy servers while users experience latency, errors or dependency failures; SLOs should represent meaningful service outcomes.

assessment_items.question: What is an error budget used for?
assessment_items.answer: It quantifies tolerated unreliability and supports decisions about delivery pace, risk and reliability work; it is not a target to consume deliberately.

assessment_items.question: Why can more alerts reduce reliability?
assessment_items.answer: Unactionable or noisy alerts consume attention, hide important signals and increase operator fatigue.

assessment_items.question: What should a useful postmortem produce?
assessment_items.answer: A shared timeline, contributing conditions, lessons and durable corrective actions that improve the system rather than blame individuals.

title: Senior Architecture/SRE Interview: Reliability, Trade-offs and Operations
summary: Senior scenarios testing architecture reasoning, SLOs, observability, incident leadership and resilience trade-offs.

questions.question: A service has 99.99 percent VM uptime but customers report frequent failures. What do you challenge first?
answer_points: component uptime is not the service objective

questions.question: Error budget is exhausted during a major feature programme. What should happen?
answer_points: make decision transparent between product and engineering

questions.question: How do you challenge a proposal for more redundancy?
answer_points: compare reliability gain against cost and new failure modes

questions.question: What makes a postmortem operationally valuable?
answer_points: verification that actions reduce recurrence or impact
